title: Introducing Long Now Labs: Where Long-term Thinking Becomes Long-term Practice
gist: Long Now Foundation launches Long Now Labs with an inaugural series, Protocols for the Long Now, co-run with the Protocol Institute. It frames 'protocolization' as a planetary force alongside globalization and financialization, and opens calls on new time standards, historical epistemic crises (now driven by LLMs and generative media), and interspecies protocols spanning humans, nature and AI agents.

insights.claim: Long Now Foundation argues that 'protocolization' is a planetary process operating alongside globalization and financialization, reshaping how societies govern themselves.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Suggests standards and coordination layers (not just physical infrastructure) as a lens for where durable value and power accrue.
insights.quote: Protocolization is a process happening alongside these forces.

insights.claim: Protocols, the social rules and conventions governing how things interact, are described as the hidden infrastructure of cooperation that mostly becomes visible only when it fails.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Protocol failure is a tail risk that is underpriced precisely because the infrastructure is invisible in normal times.
insights.quote: Most of them are invisible until they fail.

insights.claim: Long Now Foundation contends that social media algorithms, notifications, news feeds, financial transactions and agentic AI workflows are fragmenting human attention into ever-shorter time slices, worsening civilizational short-termism.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Reinforces the case that structural short-termism creates mispricing opportunities for long-horizon capital.
insights.quote: social media algorithms, digital notifications, news feeds, financial transactions, and agentic workflows slice our days into ever more urgent microseconds

insights.claim: New technologies are producing new conceptions of time, such as blood tests that report biological age and the Internet Archive's periodic timestamps of the entire internet.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Biological-age diagnostics and digital archiving are examples of consumer and institutional demand for new time-measurement products.

insights.claim: Long Now Foundation argues that social media, smartphones and LLMs over the last quarter century have eroded the traditional pathways by which societies form common knowledge, creating a current epistemic crisis driven by synthetic intelligence and generative media.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Erosion of shared truth raises demand for verification, provenance and trust infrastructure and raises political/regulatory volatility.
insights.quote: have washed out the old paths by which we used to form common knowledge

insights.claim: Epistemic cycles, in which technological disruption breaks a society's shared ability to discern truth, are framed as recurring like economic bubbles, with historical analogues from papyrus to the printing press.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Implies the AI-driven information shock may follow a historical disruption-then-adaptation pattern rather than permanent breakdown.
insights.quote: Like economic bubbles, epistemic cycles of disruption and crisis are recurring.

insights.claim: Information is framed as a civilizational raw material comparable to oil, gold, topsoil and silicon, and the protocols states use to process it are treated as critical to their longevity.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Frames information-governance capacity as a factor in state resilience and long-run country risk.
insights.quote: Like oil, gold, topsoil and silicon, information is one of civilization’s raw materials.

insights.claim: Long Now Foundation cites whales having a phonetic alphabet, rivers holding legal rights, AI agents negotiating for humans they have never met, and synthetic biology blurring species lines as signals that human-centric assumptions are dissolving.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Expanding legal personhood and agent-mediated negotiation could reshape liability, environmental regulation and contracting.
insights.quote: Rivers hold legal rights. AI agents negotiate on behalf of humans they've never met.

insights.claim: Long Now Foundation expects that governing alongside other species and synthetic intelligences will require new legal definitions of personhood and rights and new agreements on knowledge and consent across species boundaries.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Early signal of possible legal-framework shifts relevant to natural-resource, biotech and AI-agent businesses.

insights.claim: New tools such as AI are described as able to become either engines of collective intelligence or drivers of institutional decay, depending on whether shared protocols preserve human capabilities.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Highlights institutional-decay risk as a second-order outcome of AI adoption.
insights.quote: Our new tools can be engines of collective intelligence or lead to institutional decay
